s: B. The Commerce Clause.
Congress may "regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes."
The clause has gone through four eras.
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824).
Commerce is "intercourse," including navigation, and Congress's power over it is plenary within its sphere.
1887–1937: formal limits.
The Court distinguished commerce from "manufacturing," "mining" and "production" (E.C. Knight, 1895) and "direct" from "indirect" effects (Schechter Poultry, 1935).
In Hammer v. Dagenhart (1918) it struck down a child-labor law aimed at production.
1937–1995: near-plenary power.

NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel (1937), United States v. Darby (1941) and Wickard v. Filburn (1942) upheld regulation of activities with a "substantial economic effect" on interstate commerce, aggregated across all similarly situated actors.
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was sustained under this power (Heart of Atlanta Motel; Katzenbach v. McClung).
1995–present: outer limits.
Lopez struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act, and United States v. Morrison (2000) struck down the civil remedy in the Violence Against Women Act.
Gonzales v. Raich (2005) nonetheless upheld federal prohibition of home-grown medical marijuana as part of a comprehensive scheme regulating a national market.
In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), five Justices concluded the clause does not authorize compelling individuals to engage in commerce by buying insurance.
Modern Commerce Clause categories (Lopez).
Channels of interstate commerce: highways, waterways, airspace, and the movement of goods and people through them.
Instrumentalities of interstate commerce, and persons or things in interstate commerce, even when the threat comes from intrastate activity.
Activities that substantially affect interstate commerce.
Here the Court asks:
Is the regulated activity economic in nature?
If so, aggregation is permitted (Wickard; Raich).
Does the statute have a jurisdictional element tying it to interstate commerce?
Are there congressional findings?
Relevant, but not dispositive (Morrison).
How attenuated is the link between the activity and the effect on commerce?
Congress may not compel individuals to enter commerce (NFIB, five Justices).
The anti-commandeering principle.
Congress may regulate private actors directly, preempt state law, and offer states incentives.
It may not commandeer state legislatures or executive officers.
New York v. United States (1992) struck the "take title" provision for radioactive waste.
Printz v. United States (1997) held that the Brady Act could not conscript local sheriffs to run background checks.
Murphy v. NCAA (2018) held that Congress may not forbid states from repealing their own laws, so a ban on state authorization of sports gambling was invalid.
The doctrine does not bar generally applicable laws that regulate states as actors (Reno v. Condon, 2000), conditional preemption, or information-reporting duties in some contexts.
